theme: I was nearly slipping; yet I am continually with you
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 73. It is a psalm about a man who nearly lost his faith over the prosperity of the wicked. Read it as a story with a turning point, and find the verse in which everything changes.
settingTheScene: Psalm 73 is by Asaph, a leader of worship in David’s time. It opens the third book of the Psalter, and it is a perfect companion to Job. Both deal with the problem of the prosperity of the wicked and the pain of the righteous. Job came out of the book with a vision of God. Asaph comes out of the psalm with the same thing, and he tells you exactly where it happened.
observation: “Truly God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart” (v. 1). This is Asaph’s starting point.
“But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled, my steps had nearly slipped” (v. 2).
The reason: “For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” (v. 3).
The wicked have no pangs until death, and they are not in trouble as others are (vv. 4-5).
They speak with malice and set their mouths against the heavens (vv. 8-9). “They say, How can God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?” (v. 11).
Asaph says, “All in vain have I kept my heart clean and washed my hands in innocence” (v. 13).
“But when I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end” (vv. 16-17).
The wicked are on “slippery places” and are destroyed in a moment (vv. 18-19).
“Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (v. 25).
“My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (v. 26).
“But for me it is good to be near God” (v. 28).
interpretation:
The honest first confession of the psalm is worth noticing. Asaph says that he almost fell. He nearly gave up. The reason was not an intellectual doubt but an emotional one: envy. He looked at people who ignored God and seemed to be doing fine, and he felt that his own faithfulness had been a waste. Most believers have felt this.

He describes the wicked in detail. They are fat, free from pain, proud, and violent. They scoff at God. Their prosperity seems to say that there is no judgment. It is a convincing picture, and Asaph does not pretend that it is not.

Then comes verse 16. He tried to think his way through it, and it was “wearisome.” He could not reason it out. The turning point is in verse 17: “until I went into the sanctuary of God.” Something happened in God’s presence that thinking alone could not do. He saw things from the perspective of eternity. “Then I discerned their end.” The picture that looked so solid was a house on slippery ground.

The sanctuary is the place where God is worshiped, and it is where the truth about the world comes back into view. If your perspective is bent by what you see, go to where God is. This is why public worship matters.

What follows is one of the great confessions in the Psalter. “Whom have I in heaven but you?” Asaph moves from envy to desire. He no longer wants what the wicked have. He wants God. He even says that his flesh and heart may fail, and God will still be “the strength of my heart and my portion forever.” The word “portion” recalls the way the tribes were given land. His inheritance is God himself. He ends with the line that carries the whole psalm: “for me it is good to be near God.”

This is exactly where Job ended. The answer to the problem of suffering and unfairness is not a theory. It is God.
connection: Psalm 37 deals with the same theme, and so does Jeremiah 12:1. Jesus said, “What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?” (Mark 8:36). Paul says that his gain is Christ (Philippians 3:7-8). The idea of God as our portion appears in Lamentations 3:24: “The LORD is my portion, says my soul, therefore I will hope in him.”
application:
If you are envious of someone’s success, take your envy to God in worship. Go to a church service or to a quiet place and sit in his presence. Ask him to show you the end.

Pray verses 25 and 26 as your own. Say them aloud, and then ask yourself if they are honestly true. If not, ask God to make them true.

Pay attention this week to what you desire most. Ask God to teach you to want him more than anything else.
prayerPrompts: Confess any envy, and tell God where your feet have nearly slipped.
Ask him to bring you into his presence and show you the truth.
Tell him what it means that he is your portion.
